variants.reconstruction:
%n parṣam | ša mutim || šipirti (|) zikari
#note: See @bib{RN127@34–35}: “My former decipherment of the first sign overlooked the fact that the sign BAR was already used with the value @i{pár} (very rarely) in the Old Babylonian period. The revised reading and the recovery of the whole line are owed to the brilliance of Khait and Nurullin, who caught the sense of the line and made me revisit it. They read the line as @i{parṣam ša mutim piširti ikkari} and translated “a ritual of a man, an exorcism of a ploughman”, noted a parallelism between @i{parṣum} and @i{pišertum}, @i{mutum} and @i{ikkarum} and commented that the line offered “an explanation of @i{ištiāt} ‘something unique’ that Gilgamesh was supposed to make when he would meet Ḫuwawa, but we can say nothing about its exact meaning” (@bib{khait2006observations@532}). What happens when Gilgameš met Ḫuwawa was a titanic struggle so violent that the very mountain split asunder, and the logical conclusion is that the enigmatic @i{parṣam ša mutim} and the phrase that follows it allude this extraordinary act of single combat. The former phrase is easier to explain. It evokes the noble sentiment that warfare is a socio-religious duty or rite (@i{parṣum}) for able-bodied young men (@i{mutum}). This sentiment permeates ancient Mesopotamian literature: in an Old Babylonian poem about Sargon the prospect of battle is articulated by the line [@i{i}]@i{-si-nu-um ša mu-ti in-né-pu-uš} “the festival of warriors will take place” (ed. @bib{RN262@62 l. 19}); in @i{Lugale} 136 battle is ezen nam.guruš.a // @i{i-sin-ni eṭ-lu-ti} “the festival of young men”; in @i{Erra} I 51 it is said that @i{a-lak ṣēri}(edin) @i{ša eṭ-lu-ti ki-i šá i-sin-nu-um-ma} “the young men’s departure for the battlefield is like a time of festival”. Warfare is also described as @i{isinnum} “a festival” in the Agušaya poem (@bib{RN1217@76 iii 7 // 11}) and the Tukultī-Ninurta epic (@bib{RN19@99 iiia 20, 106 v 11}). While the second of the two phrases is so damaged that the reading @i{pišerti ikkari} cannot be excluded on orthographic grounds, it seemed to me on collation that a better semantic parallel with @i{parṣam ša mutim} can be obtained by reading instead @i{šipirti zikari}. In this phrase @i{šipirtum} is a synonym of @i{šiprum} “task, duty”, and thus restates @i{parṣum} but in a more mundane and less idealized way; @i{zikarum} is likewise a synonym of @i{mutum}, but less literary. In this way the line juxtaposes two phrases that display Babylonian idealism and practice respectively.”

lines.translation: #tr.en: the rite of a warrior, the task of a man.

variants.reconstruction:
%n ana rigim (|) adad | ennešu | anāku
#note: See @bib{RN127@35–36}: “The sign before @i{anāku} was revealed after cleaning to comprise only three wedges, discounting both my former decipherment @i{en-ni-iš} and Khait and Nurullin’s @i{en-né-ṭù} (@bib{khait2006observations@532–3}). I now parse the word in question from @i{ešûm}. This verb is conventionally booked as i/i class, so that the IV/1 preterite 1.sg. is expected to be @i{enneši}, as indeed it is in the Old Babylonian Narām-Sîn legend iii 8: @i{a-na-ku es-}⸢@i{se-hi}⸣ @i{en-né-ši} “I grew confused and bewildered” (ed. Westenholz 1997: 272). The late version of this text has instead forms with final /u/: in l. 88 the indicative @i{es-se-hu en-né-šú} and in l. 154 the negative imperative @i{la te-}(@i{es}5)@i{-se-eh-hu la te-en-neš-šú} “be not confused, be not bewildered” (ed. Gurney 1955, cf. Westenholz 1997: 318, 326 l. 156). The sources of the late version are tablets from Sultantepe, where an unexpected quality of final vowel would usually be shrugged off, and from Nineveh, where wrong stem vowels in final position are rare but not unknown (e.g. @bib{RN117@441 sub t}). However, the spelling @i{te-es}₅@i{-se-eh-hu} in l. 154 (MS C, Nineveh) retains in IŠ = @i{es}₅ a peculiarly Old Babylonian value, so that perhaps the spellings are there faithful to a second-millennium forerunner. Given the present attestation, on an Old Babylonian tablet, of @i{ennešu} instead of @i{enneši}, it looks as if there was indeed a time when @i{ešûm} was sometimes conjugated as a verb of the u/u class. Another case of a verb exhibiting both /u/ and /i/ in final position occurs in the next line.”

variants.reconstruction:
%n īṭū-ma | ūmu | ēmi (|) allaku | ul īde
#note: On @i{ēmi} for @i{ēma}, see @bib{RN117@240}. See also @bib{RN127@36a}: “The decipherment @i{i-}⸢@i{ṭù}⸣@i{-ma u}₄@i{-mu} and its translation as “the day went dark” presume OB @i{eṭûm} exhibits a vowel class III-@i{u}; the phrase should be compared with @akk{i-DI u₄-mu} in three first-millennium copies of @i{Ludlul} II 119, understood as @i{īṭi ūmu} by Landsberger and others: see especially Cooper 1975. Unless the phrase in the present line is plural, i.e. @i{īṭûma ūmū} (which seems improbable), this rare verb evidently exhibits both /u/ and /i/ in final position. It might thus be added to those that switched vowel classes over time (cf. @i{GAG} §87bd), but this cannot be confirmed without further attestations.” See also @bib{NABU2004-49}.

%n irt[a]hṣ[ū] | ūmam | u mušītam
#note: See @bib{RN127@36a}: “New readings reveal that this couplet as a whole is a functional counterpart of ll. 25–6: @i{mālak ūmakkal šina u šalāšim / šunu iṭḫû ana māt-Ibla}. In the later texts the variation that this tablet shows to have informed the Old Babylonian account of the journey was suppressed in favour of a standardized passage of repetition, in which each stage of the journey is introduced by the same couplet (SB IV 4 // 37 // [82] // 123–4): @i{mālak arḫi u šapatti ina šalši ūmī / iṭḫû ana šadî Labnānu}. On the textual “homogenization” of this part of the poem see further @bib{RN117@45–7}. For Ḫamran see the introduction.”

%n i[ṭ]ṭuššu[nū]ti | maṣṣ[ar]u (|) erēnim
#note: See @bib{RN127@36}: “The complete decipherment of the context shows that Ḫuwawa, not Enkidu, must be the subject of the double couplet set down in ll. 58–60, and the reading of the verb has been revised to suit this new understanding. The second sign, formerly read [@i{d}]@i{e}?, is now read DU = @i{ṭù} (cf. the shape of DU in ll. 39 and 81). A spelling @i{i-ṭù-šu-} for @i{iṭṭulšu-} does not presuppose an error, for /l/ can assimilate to a following /š/ already in Old Babylonian, as it can later: thus @i{a-ka-šu} for @i{akalšu} “his bread” in a bilingual proverb from Nippur (@bib{RN432@273 l. 2}; @bib{RN27201@§34c Ergänzungen}); and @i{na-aš-ši} for @i{nalšim} “dew” in a love lyric from the reign of Abiešuh (@bib{lambert1966divine@50 l. 11}).”
